title: What to keep from Seneca
hookLine: time, friendship, reading, calm, and honesty about failure

cards: When you move house, there's a moment with every box: keep, or let go? Not everything from the old place fits in the new one.

We're nearly done with Seneca: almost ninety days of letters and essays, and this week alone took us through gifts given and received, a grieving mother, a shameful letter from exile, a better letter to his own mother, and the long evening of his death.
Before we move on, it's time to pack.

teach.b: Here are five candidates. You'll keep three. First, time, from the very first letter, which we'll reopen tomorrow: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time."
Everything else can be taken, Seneca says, and yet time is what we let leak away most carelessly. Second, friendship. Seneca's letters are one long friendship with Lucilius.
He passes on an old line from the philosopher Hecato: if you want to be loved, love. This week added two more pictures of it: giving freely and forgetting, and receiving gladly, so the gift lands.
Third, reading. Stay with a few good writers until they become part of you, he said early on, because a mind that's everywhere is nowhere. Fourth, calm.
On Anger gave us the plainest cure: delay. Let the first rush pass, then judge.
Fifth, honesty about failure. He told Lucilius he was not wise, only less bad each day. He admitted seasickness, tears, mistakes.
And this week we saw a failure he didn't admit in the letter itself: flattery from exile. Maybe that's the strongest reason to keep this one.
Seneca shows that a person can teach well, fall short of the teaching, and still be worth reading. There's no right answer. Some people keep time, because they're always behind.
Some keep friendship, because they've been lonely. Some keep honesty about failure, because they're tired of pretending.
Choose the three that would change an ordinary Tuesday.

how: Some readers of Seneca carry a few of his themes with them rather than his whole system: guarding time, tending friendships, reading deeply, delaying anger, and admitting their own failures.

the temple where Romans went to pray
a calm, even temper kept under pressure

games.q: you can keep only three of Seneca's five. which way of choosing fits the lesson?
o: keep the three that sound most impressive.
keep the three that would change an ordinary Tuesday.
keep all five and use none.
games.why: there's no right three; the test is which ones you'd actually use on an ordinary day.

practice: Picture five boxes labeled time, friendship, reading, calm and honesty about failure, and lift each one slowly, weighing how much it matters in your life right now. Choose three, and set the other two down gently; they'll wait.
Hold your three for a while.
